qAndA.answer: The prefix "di" indicates that there are two atoms of that particular element in the compound.
qAndA.question: What does the prefix "di" indicate in a covalent compound name?

qAndA.answer: When the first element in a covalent compound formula only has one atom, the prefix "mono" is not used. It's assumed that there is one atom unless another prefix is present.
qAndA.question: In the formula CO2, why is there no prefix before "carbon"?

qAndA.answer: The name of the compound ClF3 is Chlorine trifluoride.
qAndA.question: What is the name of the compound with the formula ClF3?

text_to_speech: Hi, there my name is Dr. Scott Melideo, and in this short under 5-minute video, we will go over writing the naming and formula of a covalent compound. The assumption I am making is that you already know the different prefixes. We need to know the prefixes because for covalent compounds, there is a sharing of electrons, and the prefixes tell us how many of each element we have in a compound. We will first go from the name to the formula. Let’s look at the name, carbon monoxide. When writing the formula, the 1st element that we come across in the name is written first, which means the element that we see 2nd gets written 2nd in the formula. When the first element does not have a prefix it is assumed that there is one of them, which means for the name carbon monoxide the formula would be CO. Now it’s your turn to try writing the formula for the name dinitrogen trioxide. Pause the video to give yourself some time. The answer is N2O3. Di means 2 and tri means 3. Before we write out the name let’s go over three rules that we need to know for naming. Number 1: the element that’s 1st in the formula is going to be written 1st, and its name does not change. The element that is written 2nd in the formula will be written 2nd in the name, and the last 3 letters “ine” will be replaced with “ide” as the ending just as with ionic compounds. The 3rd rule is the prefix, which will tell us the number of each element in the molecule. To determine the prefix we look at the subscripts. Now we are ready to look at an example, CO2. The name for this would be carbon dioxide because you have one carbon and two oxygens. When we don’t see a subscript after an element the assumption is that there is one of them and because it’s the 1st element we do not need to write the prefix mono in front of the word carbon. Next, if we look at the subscript on oxygen we see that there is a 2 which means that the prefix is di. Putting it all together we get carbon dioxide. Now it is your turn with the formula ClF3. Pause the video to give yourself some time. Did you get chlorine trifluoride? There is one chlorine, so you don’t need to put mono in front of it, and for fluoride there are 3 of them, which means the prefix would be tri. I hope this was helpful! Thank you for watching!
